judge_assessment.explanation: Confirmed against the worksheet and verify.json. The sheet's directions make the pair name part of the answer in so many words -- 'Name the angle pair you are using before you compute. "Corresponding" or "alternate interior" is part of the answer, not decoration' -- and problems 2 and 5 repeat it per item ('Name the pair you used for each step', 'State the pair name used at each step'). Problems 4 and 6 additionally demand the setup in writing: 'Write the equation the angle pair justifies' and 'write the correct equation, solve for x, and give m(angle 3)'. verify.json holds fourteen entries and every one of them is an eval or solve on a number: 112/68, 65/115, 17/61, 74/106, 25/65, 30/111. No entry records a pair name and no entry records an equation, and the six middle problems carry no manual companion, so the sheet reports as fully verified when half of each answer is unchecked. The judge's second claim is also right and is the sharper form of the first: problem 1 is a pure naming task and IS declared manual, which proves the author knew naming needs a manual entry -- the same content embedded inside problems 2 through 7 was simply dropped. One gap the judge computed but did not list as a failure: problem 7 asks the student to 'find m(angle 7) and confirm that angles 7 and 8 form a linear pair', and 69 degrees is a printed answer with no verify entry at all -- the file stops at x = 30 and m(angle 2) = 111. All fourteen values recompute correctly and the problem-8 supplementary chain in the key is valid. REJECT is correct.

strengths_to_preserve: The single value-free reference diagram is a deliberate, well-reasoned design decision and the final response explains why: 'a numbered figure carrying values for one problem sits a few lines above the next problem and gets applied to it by mistake'. One eight-angle figure shows numbering only; every problem supplies its own measures in text. This should be the default pattern for any topic where all items share one configuration.

Problem 3 is the sheet's best item. It gives one measure (m(angle 4) = 65) and asks for two angles, one congruent to it and one supplementary, telling the student only that 'the names tell you which is which'. The name is not decoration there -- it is the entire discriminator between 65 and 115, and no arithmetic shortcut survives it.

The answer key opens with an explicit grading policy rather than leaving it implicit: 'The pair name is half of each answer. A correct measure with the wrong name ("vertical" where the student used corresponding angles) shows the arithmetic worked and the reasoning did not; mark the name.' It also restates the angle-numbering convention so a grader cannot misread the figure.

Multi-entry ids are used correctly for the numeric parts -- ids 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 each carry two entries, one per computed value -- so the per-value discipline is already present in this file. It is only the prose slots that were left out.

root_causes.description: There is no entry kind for a closed-vocabulary word answer, so the angle-pair name -- which is the sheet's declared subject -- has nowhere to live. The available types are all numeric or `manual`; the author used the numeric ones for the numbers and did not add manual companions for the names, and no gate noticed because every id already had a check.
evidence: verify.json: fourteen entries, all type eval or solve, all with numeric expected; the only manual entries are ids 1 and 8, which have no number at all
worksheet directions: 'Name the angle pair you are using before you compute ... part of the answer, not decoration'
worksheet problems 2 and 5 repeat the instruction per item; problems 4 and 6 add 'write the equation'
SKILL.md line 189 requires only 'at least one check' per id

root_causes.description: Problem 7 prints a third computed value that no entry covers. The item's cross-check step ('find m(angle 7) and confirm that angles 7 and 8 form a linear pair') yields 69 degrees, which is a plain numeric answer the existing `eval` type handles perfectly. It was omitted because the per-id coverage rule was already satisfied by the two entries for x and m(angle 2).
evidence: worksheet problem 7: 'Then check your answer a second way: find m(angle 7) and confirm that angles 7 and 8 form a linear pair.'
verify.json id 7: two entries only -- solve '4*x-9-(3*x+21)' -> [30] and eval '4*x-9' at x=30 -> 111
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '7. 30, 111' -- the 69 is absent from the grader's bank as well

improvements.title: Angle-pair names required by the directions need a manual entry on every problem that asks for one
improvements.proposed_change: Make `manual` a property of a response rather than of a problem, and require a companion manual entry whenever an item asks for a named classification alongside a computation. Add a lint to scripts/verify.py that scans each id's worksheet .tex segment -- and the sheet's shared directions block, which is where this sheet states the requirement -- for imperative naming markers ('name the', 'state the', 'which pair', 'write the equation', 'say why') and exits 2 listing every id that has no manual entry. On curr-306 that fires on ids 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 and would have been caught before delivery.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture whose directions block says 'Name the angle pair you are using before you compute' and whose problem 2 carries only eval entries; assert verify.py exits 2 and names problem 2. It exits 0 today because every id has a check.
improvements.expected_impact: Restores an honest manual boundary on the six middle problems, which is where this sheet's declared focus -- identifying angle pairs formed by transversals -- actually lives. Today the only two problems flagged manual are the two that contain no angle measure.
improvements.risk: Medium. Scanning the shared directions block will make the lint fire on every id of a sheet whose directions carry a blanket instruction, which is correct here but noisy on sheets where the instruction is aspirational. Warn-only for one run, then promote.

improvements.title: Problem 7's cross-check value (m(angle 7) = 69) is printed and never verified
improvements.proposed_change: Count printed response slots per problem segment in tests/check_layout.py and fail when the count exceeds the number of verify entries for that id, so a third requested value cannot ride along on an id that already has two entries. For this case add {"id": 7, "type": "eval", "expr": "180 - (4*x-9)", "at": {"x": 30}, "expected": 69} to verify.json, which also puts 69 into the answer key's Quick Answers bank where a grader can see it.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem printing three requested values with only two verify entries under its id; assert check_layout.py exits non-zero and names the missing slot. Silent today.
improvements.expected_impact: Catches the residual arithmetic that gets dropped after the 'main' answer is verified. This is the same class as the sheet's missing pair names but is fully machine-checkable, so the fix costs one JSON line.
improvements.risk: Low. Slot counting on a numeric answer is far less ambiguous than on prose; the main tuning cost is distinguishing a requested value from a value quoted back in the stem.

case_summary: The transversal mathematics is entirely correct (112/68, 65/115, x=17 with 61, 74/106, x=25 with 65, x=30 with 111, and the problem-8 alternate-interior-then-linear-pair chain), the single value-free reference figure is a genuinely good design choice with a stated rationale, and the key opens with a grading policy that tells a marker to mark the name, not just the number. The rejection is exact: the sheet declares in its own directions that the angle-pair name is 'part of the answer, not decoration', and not one of the fourteen verify entries records a name -- every entry is a number. Problem 1, which is nothing but naming, IS declared manual, which shows the mechanism was available and simply not carried into the mixed items. Beyond the judge's two hard failures, problem 7 asks for m(angle 7) = 69 as a second-method cross-check and that value appears in no verify entry and in no Quick Answers line.
